name: Carlos Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a full-stack developer, which means I work on both the screens people see and the systems behind them, at a company that makes ordering software for restaurants. When a waiter taps an order and it pops up on the kitchen screen, that's us. I start early, about eight, and most of my day I'm building features with an AI assistant doing the first draft and me fixing and checking it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building things fast and seeing them used in real kitchens, because my parents run a bakery and I grew up around that pressure. What wears me out is slow meetings and people defending old ways just because they're old. I'm 27, I live with my girlfriend Lucia, who's a dental hygienist, and on weekends I build websites for local shops using AI tools. I've saved well and own some shares, so I feel I have room to take chances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not magic, and the market priced it correctly in the end. At work I'd keep using it every day because it still saves me time. I'd tell friends the winners are the people who used it well, not the ones who waited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I enjoy what these tools can do. But my job is secure and the pay is good, so I can't complain. I'd just be a faster developer in a normal world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep growing the weekend website business, maybe from four clients to ten this year. I'd put the extra money into shares and toward a deposit, because Lucia and I want to buy a house before we marry. My parents' bakery needs a proper online ordering page too, so I'd build that for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit restless. I like a world that's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the weekend website business. Who are the clients?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly family friends: a butcher, a hairdresser, a small garage. They don't want to deal with a big agency, they want someone they know. I build each site in about two weekends with AI doing the boring parts, and charge a fair price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents' bakery, more than anything about me. Flour and energy costs keep rising, and my dad works twelve-hour days at 60. AI or no AI, I'd worry about my dad's back and the bakery's margins.

say: AI is a **useful tool**, not magic, and the market priced it right.
The winners are those who **used it well**, not the ones who waited.
think: My **job is secure** and the pay is good, so I can't complain.
I'd be a bit **disappointed**, because I enjoy what the tools can do.
do: Grow the **weekend website** business from four clients to ten.
Put extra money into **shares** and a house **deposit**.
Build a free **online ordering page** for his parents' bakery.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **restless**, liking a world that moves.
S0.quote: AI or no AI, I'd worry about my dad's back and the bakery's margins.
fieldNote: His real worry is his **parents' bakery**, not his own job.
Already runs a **side business** built on AI tools.
Plans to **buy a house** with Lucia before they marry.

steps.text: Grow the weekend website business to ten clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best chance in years for people willing to work and learn. At work I'd volunteer for every AI project going. At church and with family I'd say young people should learn the tools and a real skill, not wait for someone to look after them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. I already work the way the companies will want everyone to work, so I'd be one of the people they keep. The ones I'd worry about are colleagues who've avoided the tools for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a lead role on our team's AI work and a raise to go with it in the first few months. I'd push the weekend business harder, because small shops will want AI-built websites and ordering systems, and I'd aim for fifteen clients. I'd also set up AI ordering for my parents' bakery so my dad can stop doing it by hand at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited. It's the kind of change I've been training for without knowing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said colleagues who've avoided the tools. Who's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's Graham (a senior developer on my team), who's brilliant but refuses to touch AI. Graham has a family and a mortgage, and I'd hate to see him pushed out. I'd offer to sit with Graham for an hour a week, but I can't make him want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell young people not to wait for someone to look after them. Would you ever want the government to step in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For people truly out of options, yes, a safety net is fine. But I'd rather see money go into apprenticeships and training than straight payments, because people need to feel they earned their place.

Young people should learn **the tools** and a real skill.

Colleagues who **avoided the tools** are most at risk.

Grow the weekend business to about **fifteen clients**.
Set up **AI ordering** for his parents' bakery.

S1.quote: I'd rather see money go into apprenticeships and training than straight payments, because people need to feel they earned their place.
fieldNote: Sees steady change as a clear **opportunity** for himself.
Worries about **Graham**, a senior colleague who refuses AI.
Prefers **apprenticeships** to direct payments, in line with his values.

steps.text: Ask for the team's AI lead role and a raise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so let's be practical: own a piece of it rather than complain about it. At work I'd say every one of our jobs is changing within a year. With family I'd say we need to stick together and think like a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my developer job ends within a year or two, even with all my AI skills. If AI does almost any thinking work better and cheaper, there's no need for me in the middle. I'd have savings and shares, but I'd need a new way to earn fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the weekend business into a full company straight away, selling AI setups to restaurants and shops, because in the first year they'd be lost. I'd put some money into the bakery so my parents can buy a new oven and stay open. Lucia and I would rent for longer instead of buying, and keep a year of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but it'd be a plan for two years, not for twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't AI sell its own setups soon enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. My edge would be that shop owners trust me, not the software. That lasts a couple of years, maybe less, so I'd use those years to save and buy into something physical, like a share in the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Lucia feel about you starting a company in that moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia would worry, but Lucia's job is hands-on, in people's mouths, so it's safe until about 2031. That gives us one steady income while I take the risk. We'd agree on a limit, maybe half our savings, and not a penny more.

say: It's here, so **own a piece** of it rather than complain.
Families need to **stick together** and think like a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start, so use it. At work I'd push us to build AI products for restaurants, not just use AI to write code. With friends I'd say stop waiting for permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do very well for three or four years, then my developer job would go. That's enough time to build my own business properly while still being paid. I like those odds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job for its salary and grow the side business to about twenty clients by year two. I'd buy a house with Lucia in year one and marry the year after, as planned. By year three or four I'd leave the job and run the business full time, and I'd help modernise the bakery along the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. I know the job ends, but I've got time to build the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to the bakery. Why does it matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandfather started the bakery with one oven and a loan from my great-uncle, and it's the family's name on the sign. If I can make it run with half the hours, my dad might finally get to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your own children, if you have them? What would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn to work with their hands and with machines. And that nobody owes you a living, but family will always have your back. That's what my parents taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. At work I'd tell colleagues to start learning now while it's cheap. Online I'd share how I'm building my own business, so others see it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the best of the AGI pictures for me. I'd have years to build a business, buy a house, start a family, and be ready long before my developer job ends around 2036. I'd be 37 and running my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the company a few more years to learn everything I can and save hard, maybe 1,500 a month. I'd grow the side business steadily and make it my full-time work by 2030. I'd also buy into the bakery with my parents and bring in AI ordering and stock planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is enough for me to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots arrive around 2039, what happens to the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots might bake bread, but people will still want a bakery where the owner knows their name. We'd adapt, maybe with robots doing the heavy lifting and family serving customers. I'd rather own the robots than compete with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound very sure. Is there anything that would shake that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big companies own everything and small businesses get squeezed out, that would worry me. I don't want the government running things, but they should stop a few giants from owning all of it. Fair competition is what lets families like mine get ahead.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even with a plan, two years isn't enough to build anything that lasts. What would help is easy loans for small businesses to adapt, and real apprenticeships so people can retrain while earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who ends up owning all this. If a handful of giant companies own the machines, families like mine are just customers forever. I want my children to inherit a bakery, not a subscription.

headlineQuote: I want my children to inherit a bakery, not a subscription.
portrait: A **27-year-old** full-stack developer on restaurant ordering software who uses **AI daily**.
Lives with **Lucia**, a dental hygienist, and runs a weekend website business.
Traditional and family-minded, rooted in his parents' **bakery**.
Calm in the plateau and steady change, **anxious** only if AGI comes in two years.
Plans to **own a business** rather than be replaced, and to buy into the bakery.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years can't build anything that **lasts**.
whatWouldHelp: Easy **loans** for small businesses to adapt.
Real **apprenticeships** so people retrain while earning.
